title: A First-principles Computational Framework for Quantum Decoherence in Complex Diamond Spin Environments
authors: Huijin Park, Ha-young Jeong, Hyeonsu Kim, Christoph Findler, Fedor Jelezko, Sangwon Oh, Junghyun Lee, Giulia Galli, Hosung Seo
abstract: Quantum decoherence induced by defects remains a major limitation for solid-state quantum technologies, yet predicting decoherence in realistic materials remains computationally challenging. Complex defect populations are often approximated as homogeneous spin baths, obscuring the role of defect-specific electronic structure and spin dynamics. Here, we develop a predictive framework for decoherence in diamond by combining first-principles electronic-structure calculations, quantum many-body spin-bath simulations, and experimental validation. The framework incorporates defect-resolved spin Hamiltonians and heterogeneous spin baths containing multiple paramagnetic defect species. Using diamond nitrogen-vacancy ensembles as a model platform, we investigate mixed nitrogen-, vacancy-, and hydrogen-related defect environments. We show that decoherence depends not only on defect density but also on defect identity and bath composition, whose distinct electronic structures, hyperfine interactions, and spin dynamics produce different coherence behavior. Heterogeneous defect populations can either suppress or enhance decoherence, producing trends unexplained by homogeneous-bath models. Magnetic-field-dependent Hahn-echo measurements on samples with different defect concentrations validate the framework. The calculations reproduce the observed coherence times and stretched-exponential decay behavior across a broad magnetic-field range and identify vacancy-related defects as critical contributors beyond the conventionally assumed P1 spin bath. By linking atomistic defect properties to quantum coherence, our framework provides a predictive route for identifying hidden defect environments and optimizing decoherence in defect-based quantum materials.
summary: This work introduces a first-principles computational framework to accurately model quantum decoherence in diamond by treating complex, heterogeneous defect environments. By combining DFT with spin-bath simulations, the authors show that individual defect types critically influence coherence times, offering a predictive tool for optimizing quantum materials.
main_problem: Predicting quantum decoherence in realistic solid-state materials is computationally challenging because complex defect environments are often inaccurately modeled as simple homogeneous spin baths.
main_result: The study demonstrates that decoherence depends critically on the specific identity and composition of defects, showing that heterogeneous bath effects can significantly alter coherence times compared to predictions from simpler models.
method: A predictive framework combining first-principles electronic structure calculations (DFT) with quantum many-body spin-bath simulations is developed and validated against magnetic-field-dependent Hahn-echo measurements.
model_or_system: The system uses diamond containing Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) ensembles as the central qubit, interacting with a heterogeneous bath of multiple paramagnetic defects (e.g., N-, V-, H-related species).
key_observables: Quantum coherence time ($T_2^*$), decoherence decay behavior (stretched exponential), and field dependence.
important_parameters: Defect identity, defect concentration, hyperfine interaction parameters, and magnetic field strength.
main_assumptions: The framework moves beyond homogeneous bath approximations by incorporating defect-resolved spin Hamiltonians and heterogeneous interactions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the central spin model used to compute decoherence dynamics of an NV center interacting with a PM defect spin bath environment.
paper_structure: The paper develops a computational framework, applies it to model decoherence in diamond using various defects, and validates its predictions by reproducing experimental coherence times across different magnetic fields.
why_interesting: It provides a crucial link between atomistic material science (DFT of defect structure) and fundamental quantum dynamics (decoherence), which is vital for designing robust solid-state qubits.
